creator: Bogdan (@Bogzabs96)
title: How I'd start AI ads if I had zero today (Full 30-Day Playbook)
summary: An agency operator who went from 26 to 111 AI ad concepts a month lays out a four-week on-ramp for a brand running no AI ads. Every AI ad starts from an already-proven message, and AI changes only the visual. Week 1 is a fast static session of native statics, competitor clones and us-vs-them, built with GPT Image 2, Claude captions and Canva fixes. Week 2 remakes the best existing script word-for-word as a Pixar-style animated ad through a Claude Code skill. Week 3 adds a second visual style and a Suno song ad, with specific rules for scripting and prompting it. Week 4 turns this into a system: parallel production, a per-ad cost log, per-step timing, and remaking winners in new looks. He publishes real per-ad generation costs, from about $7 to $240 with an average of about $30. He warns against skipping a 'what good looks like' reference set, starting with photoreal AI drama, leaving automations unwatched, and making ads look AI for its own sake.
recencySignals: Published 2026-11-05. Names GPT Image 2 (via Higgsfield), Kling, Suno, Claude Code skills, and Canva. Refers to an April-to-September (2026) ramp and a 30 September parallel run. Says photoreal 'soap opera' AI is not yet ready. All are current platform and model capability claims.

tactics.claim: Start every AI ad from a message that is already proven (a winning angle, script or persona), so AI changes only the picture. Then feed each winner back in for a new look: 'winner in, new look out' is the whole engine.
tactics.mechanism: The risky variable in a new ad is the message. Holding it fixed means only the visual is being tested, and on Meta a new look is what buys new reach.
tactics.evidence: A strategist remade a Pixar winner in claymation and called it 'literally a whole new ad'. The rest is the team's own scale-up from 26 to 111 AI concepts.

rscFit.reasoning: Sound and directly applicable to RSC's Trybe UGC winners, but the claim is already recorded.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate. marketing-ai-broll-generation already holds 'Rebuild an existing talking-head winner as a second ad by keeping the script, audio and messaging identical and changing only the visuals'. marketing-paid-creative-testing already holds 'dissect a breakthrough ad… produce many deliberate iterations… porting the winner's angle and storyline into a different format'.

tactics.claim: In week 1, put three people in a room for an hour or two, make 20-30 statics across 4-5 angles, launch them all, and read which angle gets the cheapest clicks.
tactics.mechanism: Statics are the fastest creative to produce, so they give the earliest read on which angles buyers react to while video is still being built.
tactics.evidence: Three of their people made 20-30 statics in about an hour and found winners, 'even top spenders'.

rscFit.reasoning: Producing statics fast is already covered. The read it prescribes is cheapest clicks, which the existing measurement skill explicitly bans as a performance verdict. Launching 20-30 at once also runs into the recorded doom-cycle rule.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate, and in conflict with recorded rules. It matches marketing-paid-creative-testing 'Start creative testing with static ads rather than video' and the raw-volume native statics claim. It conflicts with marketing-paid-media-measurement 'never treat click-through rate as a performance verdict' and with marketing-paid-creative-testing 'Stop continuously launching new ads alongside a campaign that is already running'.

tactics.claim: The week-1 static mix should be native camera-roll photos with story-style captions, one or two clones of a competitor static that is clearly working rebuilt with your product, and one us-vs-them.
tactics.mechanism: Native formats and already-converting layouts lower the failure rate of a first static batch.

rscFit.reasoning: The native and us-vs-them parts are already held. The competitor-clone part crosses a recorded line.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-paid-creative-testing's eight named native formats (candid photo, us-vs-them). Cloning a competitor static with your product swapped in contradicts marketing-ai-product-imagery 'never upload a competitor's asset and ask the model to swap your face or product into it'. The permitted version, recreating an out-of-category ad, is already recorded.

tactics.claim: Route any static or starting frame that shows your product to the image model that renders the packaging label correctly most often (currently GPT Image 2). Use the LLM only for captions and Canva only for the last 10% fix.
tactics.mechanism: A wrong label is the most common reason a product render cannot ship. Picking the model on label fidelity cuts regeneration and correction rounds. A static dropped from 90 minutes and three revision rounds to minutes.
tactics.evidence: The team's own before/after production time (90 minutes and three rounds down to minutes). The label-accuracy claim is their observation.

rscFit.reasoning: RSC's ad-batch pipeline renders statics of labelled deodorant, lotion and balm tins, where legible on-pack text matters. This is the platform-mechanics class (fast decay). The model ranking is current as of November 2026 but should be re-checked within months. It is runnable today by the operator.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-product-imagery
targetSkill.description: Use when generating ad statics, listing images or video starting frames that show the real product and its label, and you need to choose which image model to run and when to finish by hand. Covers routing label-bearing frames to the model with the best packaging-text fidelity, captions written separately in the LLM, and a final Canva pass for near-misses.

tactics.claim: Choose the animation style to match the gravity of the problem the ad addresses. Pixar-style carries emotion for a serious problem. A health problem rendered in Lego reads as a joke.
tactics.mechanism: The visual style sets the emotional register before a word lands. A style that undercuts the problem's seriousness makes the claim feel unserious and kills belief.
tactics.evidence: Their own pattern: Pixar is 'usually the style that works best for us' on serious problems.

rscFit.reasoning: RSC already runs AI-generated video (Gemini Omni), so picking a style is a live decision. Skin and odour problems span light (sweaty commute) to tender (eczema-prone dry skin), so the gravity-to-style match matters per angle. This is a durable principle, and the operator can run it today.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-video-ad-production
targetSkill.description: Use when turning a proven ad script into an AI-generated video and deciding which visual style (Pixar-style 3D, claymation, crochet, cartoon character, AI presenter, photoreal) it should be rendered in. Covers matching the style's emotional register to how serious the buyer's problem is.

tactics.claim: Treat the approved brief as locked. When the AI pipeline splits a script into scenes and prompts, it must never rewrite the copy.
tactics.mechanism: The whole bet rests on reusing a proven message. Any wording the model 'improves' during scene breakdown silently turns a one-variable test into a two-variable one.
tactics.evidence: assertion only (stated as a rule of their SOP)

rscFit.reasoning: This is the guardrail that makes re-rendering a Trybe UGC winner's script in a new AI style a clean test. It applies to any skill-driven pipeline the operator runs. It is a durable principle and runnable now.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-video-ad-production
targetSkill.description: Use when an LLM or director skill is converting an approved ad script into scenes, shot lists or generation prompts. Covers instructing it that the script copy is locked and verifying the spoken lines survive verbatim, so a re-skinned winner tests only the visual.

tactics.claim: Before anything is animated, check the generated characters and frames against the strategic details in the brief. A senior dog that must look senior, or a 60-year-old lead who renders as 35, decides whether the ad wins.
tactics.mechanism: The buyer's self-recognition depends on the on-screen subject matching their age and situation. Image models drift toward young, generic subjects, and catching that at the still-frame stage is cheap while catching it after animation is expensive.
tactics.evidence: Their own failed and corrected examples (the senior dog, the 60-year-old lead).

rscFit.reasoning: RSC's body-cream buyers skew older than models' default subjects, so age and skin-condition fidelity in AI frames is a real risk. Existing claims settle the storyboard but do not name this demographic-fidelity gate. It is a durable principle and runnable now.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-video-ad-production
targetSkill.description: Use when approving AI-generated characters and starting frames before sending them to a video model. Covers a gate that checks each frame against the brief's strategic specifics (buyer age, life stage, visible condition, pet or prop details) and regenerates mismatches before any credits go to animation.

tactics.claim: Launch the first AI video with three hook variants.
tactics.mechanism: The hook decides whether the proven body ever gets watched, so varying it gives the new look several entry points.
tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-paid-creative-testing 'Test 3-6 hook variations per creative test'.

tactics.claim: In week 3, render the same script in a second visual world (claymation, crochet, a cartoon character, an AI presenter) so an account that has run the same creator in the same kitchen stops looking like one ad.
tactics.mechanism: Visually distinct creatives are treated as new ads and reach new pockets of the audience. Look-alikes cluster together.
tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-paid-creative-testing 'Judge an image batch by visual distinctness… only a new scene, subject, format… is a genuinely new ad' and the port-the-winner-into-a-different-format claim.

tactics.claim: Run AI song ads (Suno). Write a normal direct-response script with no rhymes and let the music model turn it into a song.
tactics.mechanism: A sung ad reads as entertainment and is sticky, while the unrhymed DR script keeps every selling point and claim intact. Forcing rhymes would bend the copy away from what sells.
tactics.evidence: One song ad for a new client went from $500 to over $12K spend in 3 days and passed the account's ROAS target within 5 days. Song ads are now their most-produced AI format. Generation costs about $24-29 per ad.

rscFit.reasoning: This format is new to every existing skill. It suits a low-ticket, everyday consumable (deodorant, lotion, lip balm), where a catchy sung benefit fits the category. At about $25-30 per ad it costs less than a day of RSC's ~$50/day test budget. The operator can produce it alone today with existing Trybe UGC or AI visuals. Launching it in the account is a recommendation to David Parrotino. The evidence is a single vendor case, which keeps the score off the top of the range. It is a platform-mechanics-adjacent format, current as of November 2026.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-voiceover-production
targetSkill.description: Use when making a sung or jingle-style video ad with an AI music generator such as Suno, or deciding whether a proven ad script could run as a song. Covers keeping the script as unrhymed direct-response copy and letting the model set it to music.

tactics.claim: In a song ad, the hook must open the first verse, and the style prompt must end with 'vocals start immediately, no instrumental intro', because the model sings intros softly.
tactics.mechanism: Music models default to an instrumental lead-in and soft opening vocals. That spends the first seconds of a feed placement, where the scroll decision is made, on nothing audible.
tactics.evidence: The team's production rules from their Suno ads (assertion from practice).

rscFit.reasoning: A precise and cheap fix that decides whether a song ad survives its first two seconds in Reels and feed, where RSC posts daily. It is platform mechanics (fast decay): a model-behaviour quirk that is current now and should be re-checked as Suno versions change. It is runnable today.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-voiceover-production
targetSkill.description: Use when writing the lyrics and style prompt for an AI-generated song ad and the opening seconds come out quiet or instrumental. Covers putting the hook in the first verse and ending the style prompt with an explicit no-intro, vocals-immediately instruction.

tactics.claim: Run several AI ads in parallel, each in its own chat and folder, reviewing one while another generates.
tactics.mechanism: Generation time is idle time. Isolating each ad's context lets one operator keep two to five productions moving at once.
tactics.evidence: Their SOP asks editors for 2-3 at a time, and he ran two animation ads in parallel on 30 September.

rscFit.reasoning: Useful for throughput, but it restates a recorded workflow.

tactics.rejectReason: Near-duplicate of marketing-ai-broll-generation 'Run image generation and video generation in two separate browser tabs side by side so you can queue a generation in one while working in the other', together with marketing-ai-prompt-craft's one-thread-per-recurring-job claim.

tactics.claim: Keep a production log with one row per ad code: image cost, clip cost, rework cost, total, and start/end time of each step. Review it weekly to catch automations silently burning credits.
tactics.mechanism: Without per-ad cost and time there is no answer to 'is AI actually cheaper?' and no input to a creative-return benchmark. The weekly review catches runaway auto-generation, which once burned their credits unnoticed.
tactics.evidence: Their published cost log (from $6.67 to $239.59 per ad) and an auto-generation setting that burned credits until someone caught it.

rscFit.reasoning: RSC runs a pay-per-generation AI pipeline (Gemini Omni video, the ad-batch renderer). The existing claim 'attributed revenue per concept divided by the cost to produce it' needs exactly this denominator, and nothing records how to capture it. Per-step timing is the solo operator's own capacity budget. It is a durable principle, runnable today in a spreadsheet.

targetSkill.name: marketing-paid-media-measurement
targetSkill.description: Use when producing AI-generated ads or statics and you need to know what each one cost in credits and hours, or whether AI creative is paying back. Covers a per-ad-code production log (generation, rework, total, step timings) reviewed weekly for runaway automation spend, feeding the revenue-per-concept benchmark.

tactics.claim: Do not start with photoreal AI drama. Start with stylised formats (Pixar-style, claymation, songs), because realistic AI drama comes back with jarring cuts and robotic voices and needs heavy rework.
tactics.mechanism: Current video models fail most visibly at realistic human acting and dialogue. Viewers forgive stylised worlds, while they read photoreal flaws as fake, so stylised formats ship with far less rework per dollar.
tactics.evidence: Their realistic AI drama ad cost $239.59, versus about $20-30 for Pixar and Suno ads, and needed about 45% rework.

rscFit.reasoning: RSC's Gemini Omni output includes dialogue scenes, so this tells the operator where to point first attempts. It is platform mechanics (fast decay) and reflects November 2026 model capability, so it should be revisited as models improve. It is runnable today.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-video-ad-production
targetSkill.description: Use when choosing what kind of AI video ad to make first or deciding whether a photoreal dramatised scene is worth the credits. Covers defaulting to stylised formats (Pixar-style, claymation, song) over realistic AI drama, which currently carries far higher rework and cost per usable ad.

tactics.claim: Before producing, save about ten AI ads you would be proud to run, to define what good looks like.
tactics.mechanism: Without a shown quality bar, the first outputs drift far from the viral references being imitated.
tactics.evidence: Their first Pixar ads in April 'didn't look anything like the viral ones we were copying'.
tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-short-form-video-production 'Record by modelling a reference video that already crushed in the exact format you are making' and marketing-ai-product-imagery 'build the reference board from ads that are already converting'.

tactics.claim: Run a strip-away test on every AI ad: remove the animation and ask whether it is still a real ad. If a phone could have shot the hook, the AI version needs a reason to exist, because cute is not proof.
tactics.mechanism: AI novelty can mask a weak message. Stripping the visual exposes whether the script carries a selling argument, and the phone test stops credits being spent where cheaper real footage would read as more credible.

rscFit.reasoning: Useful as a pre-ship gate, since RSC has abundant approved Trybe UGC that could carry many hooks a phone could shoot. It partly overlaps with 'Shoot the real footage you can actually get, then use AI only for shots you could not capture', but it adds a ship/no-ship audit of the finished ad. It is a durable principle and runnable now.

targetSkill.name: marketing-ai-video-ad-production
targetSkill.description: Use when reviewing a finished AI-generated video ad before it ships, or deciding whether a concept should be AI at all. Covers the strip-away test (is it still a real ad without the animation?) and the phone test (could real creator UGC have shot this hook more credibly?).

tactics.claim: Build AI ads through a Claude Code skill pipeline: script split into scenes, scenes approved, then characters and starting frames, clips, rough cut, and a final edit in CapCut.
tactics.mechanism: A staged, approved pipeline cuts brief-to-rough-cut from 3-6 hours to about 40 minutes of machine time.

rscFit.reasoning: Applicable, but every stage is already recorded.

tactics.rejectReason: Duplicate of marketing-ai-video-ad-production 'Install a reusable director skill… per-cut shot list' and 'Build an AI video ad in five fixed stages in order — script outline, character generation, storyboard, video generation, edit'.

tactics.claim: By day 30, use the angle reads, style results, cost log and timing to decide how much of monthly creative should be AI.
tactics.mechanism: Stated as a decision outcome, not a mechanism.
tactics.evidence: Their own growth from 26 to 111 AI concepts.

rscFit.reasoning: This is a summary of the month rather than a separate tactic. Its inputs are captured by the adopted cost-log tactic.

tactics.rejectReason: No distinct mechanism. It restates the outputs of the other tactics as a planning conclusion, and its measurement inputs are covered by the adopted production-log tactic and the existing creative-return benchmark in marketing-paid-media-measurement.
